title: Croatia, filed under other countries
eyebrow: What a map built from one collection cannot see
dek: The research map was built from FamilySearch's Croatian church-book collection. Croatian places also sit inside Italian, Hungarian, Austrian and Slovenian collections, under names the map has never heard of.
lead:
This archive's map says it shows *«every parish in Croatia whose registers are on film»*. **It does not, and it never did.** It shows every parish in **one collection** — *Croatia, Church Books, 1516–1994* — plus three smaller sources this archive added by hand.

FamilySearch publishes **3,488 collections**. The whole list was walked on 15 September 2026 and filtered for anything that could touch a Croatian place. What came back is below — **three of them are now on the map** — and the short version is: **a Croatian town is filed wherever the state that kept its registers happened to be**, under the name that state used. Čakovec is under *Csáktornya*, in a Hungarian county, in a collection named for Slovenia.

found.title: Croatia, Church Books, 1516–1994
found.what: The collection the research map is built from — 1,333 parishes, 5,482 volumes.
found.note: Ours. Everything else on this page is not.

found.title: Croatia, Delnice Deanery Catholic Church Books, 1571–1926
found.what: A second Croatian church-book collection, for the Delnice deanery in Gorski kotar — the mountain country directly inland from Crikvenica and Bribir.
found.note: **It browses by film number, not by parish**, so the place-walk that built the research map could never have found it. Six reels, ~3,485 images, **no parish structure at all** — they hang on Delnice itself rather than pretending to a precision the collection does not have.

found.title: Italy, Pola and Trieste, Catholic Church Records, 1593–1941
found.what: Seven Istrian parishes under «Pola» — **Buie, Cittanova d'Istria, Portole, Verteneglio, Materada, Isola d'Istria, Pirano** — and four under Trieste.
found.note: **Five of those seven are in Croatia today** — Buje, Novigrad, Oprtalj, Brtonigla and Materada — and all of them are now on the map, each under **both** names. **36 volumes across 9 places.**

found.title: Slovenia, Prekmurje and Međimurje, Civil Registers, 1895–1918
found.what: Two roots, **Vas** and **Zala** — Hungarian counties. Under Zala are **33 registration districts**, and nearly all of them are Croatian towns in Međimurje.
found.note:
**Csáktornya is Čakovec. Perlak is Prelog. Nedelicz is Nedelišće. Stridó is Štrigova. Kottori is Kotoriba. Légrád is Legrad.** A Croatian county's civil registers, under Hungarian place names, in a collection named for Slovenia.

**Now on the map: 46 places, 365 volumes**, each on the same dot as its modern name and carrying the catalogue's spelling in «also written» — because that is the name you must search for to find the book.

found.title: Italy, Udine, Civil Registration (State Archive), 1806–1815, 1871–1911
found.what: The Carnia comuni — Mione and Ovaro among them.
found.note: Already a provider here, as **fs-it**, with 26 places.

found.title: Italy, Trieste, Trieste, Civil Registration (Tribunale), 1924–1939
found.what: Duino, Muggia, San Dorligo della Valle, San Pelagio, Sgonico, Trieste.
found.note: All in Italy or Slovenia today. **Nothing Croatian** — checked so it need not be checked again.

found.title: Italy, Trieste, Civil Registration (State Archive), 1924–1944
found.what: A single root, and it is **Slovenia**.
found.note: Nothing Croatian at the top level.

found.title: Austria, Catholic Church Records, 1565–2007
found.what: **6.85 million records, 17.4 million persons — and no browse tree at all.** It is a name index, not a filmed collection, so it cannot be walked by place.
found.note:
**It does not cover the Austrian Littoral.** Searched inside the collection: **289 Defranceschi records**, and every named place among them is Tyrolean — *Bozen, Salorno, Tirolo, St. Florian bei Linz*. Not one in Istria, Gorizia or Trieste. The same for three Istrian surnames tested alongside: **Sestan** (Zwettl, Longomosso, Feldkirch), **Kostesich** (Bozen), **Miškulin** (Bozen).

**So the hole stays open.** Gračišće, Gologorica and Pićan are not here either, and this was the most promising place they could have been.

*Two things worth keeping anyway.* **There is a whole Tyrolean Defranceschi population** — 289 records around Bozen and Salorno — which is a separate family of the same name and a standing warning against arguing from a surname. And one record reads *«Vukovar, Sriem, Croatia, Austria»*, so **Slavonian places do appear in this collection** even though Istrian ones do not.

found.title: Hungary, Civil Registration, 1895–1980
found.what: **33 Hungarian counties** — Abaúj-Torna, Arad, Bács-Bodrog, Baranya … Vas, Veszprém, Zala. **Not one Croatian-Slavonian county, and no Fiume.**
found.note:
**It does not reach Croatia, and the reason is constitutional rather than archival.**

Hungary introduced civil registration in **1895**. **Croatia-Slavonia did not.** Under the Nagodba it ran its own administration and **kept the parish registers as the legal civil record until 1946** — which is why FamilySearch's Croatian collection is *church books*, and why there is no Croatian civil-registration collection anywhere to find.

**And it explains Međimurje.** Međimurje's civil registers exist from 1895 because Međimurje was administered as part of **Zala county — as Hungary proper, not as Croatia**. That is the whole anomaly.

*Checked rather than assumed:* Zala here holds **235 districts** and **not one** of Csáktornya, Perlak, Nedelicz, Stridó, Kottori or Légrád — they are in the Slovenia-titled collection instead, so the two do not overlap. The **16 Defranceschi** records inside are **Budapest, Esztergom and Sopron**.

found.title: Italy, Gorizia, Census, 1742–1895
found.what: No browse tree — an index-only collection.
found.note: Searchable by name, not walkable by place.

close:
**Three of these are now on the map** — *Pola and Trieste*, *Prekmurje and Međimurje*, and *Delnice* — as their own providers, each place shown under **the name its catalogue uses as well as the name it goes by today**. Čakovec and «Csáktornya» are one dot.

**And the merge paid for itself immediately.** With the parish books and the Hungarian civil registers on the same marker, Čakovec shows a **four-year gap in 1891–1894 across births, marriages and deaths** — the interval between the church books closing and civil registration opening. **Neither catalogue could show that on its own.**

**The lesson is about method rather than about any one collection.** A map built from a collection named for a country will show the places that country's archives filmed, and nothing else. **The border moved five times in a century and the paperwork did not follow it.** Every place on this family's ground was, at some point, filed by Venice, by Vienna, by Budapest, by Rome and by Zagreb — and FamilySearch files by whoever kept the book.
